'''Torsten Carleman''' (8 July 1892, Visseltofta, [[Osby Municipality]] – 11 January 1949, [[Stockholm]]), born '''Tage Gillis Torsten Carleman''', was a [[Sweden|Swedish]] [[mathematician]], known for his results in [[classical analysis]] and its applications. As the director of the [[Mittag-Leffler Institute]] for more than two decades, Carleman was the most influential mathematician in Sweden.

==Work==

The dissertation of Carleman under [[Erik Albert Holmgren]], as well as his work in the early 1920s, was devoted to [[singular integral equations]]. He developed the [[spectral theory]] of [[integral operator]]s with ''Carleman kernels'', that is, [[integral transform|kernels]] ''K''(''x'',&nbsp;''y'') such that ''K''(''y'',&nbsp;''x'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;<span style="text-decoration: overline">''K''(''x'',&nbsp;''y'')</span> for [[Almost everywhere|almost every]] (''x'',&nbsp;''y''), and 
:<math> \int | K(x, y) |^2 dy < \infty </math>
for almost every ''x''.<ref>{{cite book|mr=0605488|last=Dieudonné|first=Jean|author-link=Jean Dieudonné|title=History of functional analysis|series=North-Holland Mathematics Studies|volume=49|publisher=North-Holland Publishing Co.|location=Amsterdam&ndash;New York|year=1981|isbn=0-444-86148-3|pages=[https://archive.org/details/historyoffunctio0000dieu/page/168 168&ndash;171]|url=https://archive.org/details/historyoffunctio0000dieu/page/168}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|mr=0028526|last=Ahiezer|first=N. I.|author-link=Naum Akhiezer|title=Integral operators with Carleman kernels|language= Russian|journal=Uspekhi Mat. Nauk|volume=2|year=1947|issue=5(21)|pages=93&ndash;132|url=http://mi.mathnet.ru/umn6983}}</ref>

In the mid-1920s, Carleman developed the theory of [[quasi-analytic function]]s. He proved the necessary and sufficient condition for quasi-analyticity, now called the [[Denjoy–Carleman theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal|mr=0006354|last=Mandelbrojt|first=S.|author-link=Szolem Mandelbrojt|title=Analytic functions and classes of infinitely differentiable functions|journal=Rice Inst. Pamphlet|volume= 29|year=1942|issue=1}}</ref> As a corollary, he obtained a [[Carleman's condition|sufficient condition]] for the determinacy of the [[moment problem]].<ref>{{Cite book |mr=0184042 |first=N. I. |last=Akhiezer |author-link=Naum Akhiezer|title=The Classical Moment Problem and Some Related Questions in Analysis |publisher=Oliver & Boyd |year=1965 }}</ref> As one of the steps in the proof of the Denjoy–Carleman theorem in {{harvtxt|Carleman|1926}}, he introduced the [[Carleman inequality]]
:<math> \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n\right)^{1/n} \le e \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n,</math>
valid for any sequence of non-negative real numbers ''a''<sub>''k''</sub>.<ref>{{cite journal|mr=1820809|last1=Pečarić|first1=Josip|last2=Stolarsky|first2=Kenneth B.|title=Carleman's inequality: history and new generalizations|journal=[[Aequationes Mathematicae]]|volume= 61|year=2001|issue=1&ndash;2|pages=49&ndash;62|doi=10.1007/s000100050160|s2cid=121175099}}</ref>

At about the same time, he established the ''[[Carleman formulae]]'' in [[complex analysis]], which reconstruct an [[analytic function]] in a domain from its values on a subset of the boundary. He also proved a generalisation of [[Jensen's formula]], now called the [[Jensen–Carleman formula]].<ref name=carlson>{{cite journal|last=Carlson|first=F.|author-link=Fritz Carlson|title=Torsten Carleman|language=French|journal=Acta Math.|volume=82|year=1950|issue=1|pages=i&ndash;vi|mr=1555457|doi=10.1007/BF02398273|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the 1930s, independently of [[John von Neumann]], he discovered the [[mean ergodic theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal|mr=1546100|doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-39-00501-6|zbl= 0021.23501|last=Wiener|first=N.|author-link=Norbert Wiener|title=The ergodic theorem|journal=Duke Math. J.|volume=5|year=1939|issue=1|pages=1&ndash;18}}</ref> Later, he worked in the theory of [[partial differential equation]]s, where he introduced the ''[[Carleman estimates]]'',<ref>{{cite book|mr=0934297|last=Kenig|first=Carlos E.|chapter=Carleman estimates, uniform Sobolev inequalities for second-order differential operators, and unique continuation theorems|title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Vol. 1, 2 (Berkeley, Calif., 1986)|pages=948&ndash;960|publisher=Amer. Math. Soc.|location=Providence, RI|year=1987}}</ref> and found a way to study the spectral asymptotics of [[Schrödinger operator]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|mr=0510064|last=Clark|first=Colin|title=The asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for elliptic boundary value problems|journal=SIAM Rev.|volume=9|year=1967|issue=4|pages=627&ndash;646|doi=10.1137/1009105|bibcode=1967SIAMR...9..627C }}</ref>

In 1932, following the work of [[Henri Poincaré]], [[Erik Ivar Fredholm]], and [[Bernard Koopman]], he devised the ''[[Carleman embedding]]'' (also called ''Carleman linearization''), a way to embed a finite-dimensional system of nonlinear differential equations {{frac|d'''u'''|d''t''}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''P'''('''u''') for '''u''':&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''', where the components of '''P'''  are polynomials in '''u''', into an infinite-dimensional system of linear differential equations.<ref>{{cite book|mr=1178493|last1=Kowalski|first1=Krzysztof|last2=Steeb|first2=Willi-Hans|title=Nonlinear dynamical systems and Carleman linearization|url=https://archive.org/details/nonlineardynamic00kowa|url-access=limited|publisher=World Scientific Publishing Co., Inc|location=River Edge, NJ|year=1991|isbn=981-02-0587-2|page=[https://archive.org/details/nonlineardynamic00kowa/page/n7 7]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr=1296251|last=Kowalski|first=K|title=Methods of Hilbert spaces in the theory of nonlinear dynamical systems|publisher=World Scientific Publishing Co., Inc.|location=River Edge, NJ|year=1994|isbn=981-02-1753-6}}</ref>

In 1933 Carleman published a short proof of what is now called the [[Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Sur une inégalité différentielle dans la théorie des fonctions analytiques|journal=[[Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences]]|date=April 3, 1933|volume=196|pages=995–7|url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3148d/f995.image.langFR|author=Torsten Carleman}}</ref>
This theorem states that the number of asymptotic values attained by an [[entire function]] of order ρ along curves in the [[complex plane]] going outwards toward infinite absolute value is less than or equal to 2ρ.

In 1935, Torsten Carleman introduced a generalisation of [[Fourier transform]], which foreshadowed the work of [[Mikio Sato]] on [[hyperfunction]]s;<ref name=kiselman>{{cite book|mr=2068535|last=Kiselman|first=Christer O.|chapter=Generalized Fourier transformations: The work of Bochner and Carleman viewed in the light of the theories of Schwartz and Sato|title=Microlocal analysis and complex Fourier analysis|pages=166&ndash;185|publisher=World Sci. Publ.|location=River Edge, NJ|year=2002|url=http://www2.math.uu.se/~kiselman/ws-p8-50x6-00.pdf}}</ref> his notes were published in {{harvtxt|Carleman|1944}}. He considered the functions ''f'' of at most polynomial growth, and showed that every such function can be decomposed as ''f''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''f''<sub>+</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''f''<sub>&minus;</sub>, where ''f''<sub>+</sub> and ''f''<sub>&minus;</sub> are analytic in the upper and lower half planes, respectively, and that this representation is essentially unique. Then he defined the Fourier transform of  (''f''<sub>+</sub>,&nbsp;''f''<sub>&minus;</sub>) as another such pair (''g''<sub>+</sub>,&nbsp;''g''<sub>&minus;</sub>). Though conceptually different, the definition coincides with the one given later by [[Laurent Schwartz]] for [[distribution (mathematics)#Tempered distributions and Fourier transform|tempered distributions]].<ref name=kiselman/> Carleman's definition gave rise to numerous extensions.<ref name=kiselman/><ref>{{cite book|mr=1180762|last=Singh|first=U. N.|chapter=The Carleman-Fourier transform and its applications|title=Functional analysis and operator theory|pages=181&ndash;214|series=Lecture Notes in Math.|volume=1511|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|year=1992}}</ref>

Returning to [[mathematical physics]] in the 1930s, Carleman gave the first proof of global existence for [[Boltzmann's equation]] in the [[kinetic theory of gases|kinetic theory]] of gases (his result applies to the space-homogeneous case).<ref>{{citation|mr=2509759|last=Cercignani|first=C.|author-link=Carlo Cercignani|title=134 years of Boltzmann equation. Boltzmann's legacy|pages=107&ndash;127|series=ESI Lect. Math. Phys.|publisher=Eur. Math. Soc.|location=Zürich|year=2008|doi=10.4171/057-1/8}}</ref> The results were published posthumously in {{harvtxt|Carleman|1957}}.

Carleman supervised the Ph.D. theses of Ulf Hellsten, Karl Persson (Dagerholm), [[Åke Pleijel]] and (jointly with [[Fritz Carlson]]) of [[Hans Rådström]].

==Life==
Carleman was born in [[Visseltofta]] to Alma Linnéa Jungbeck and Karl Johan Carleman, a school teacher.<ref name=carlson/> He studied at [[Katedralskolan, Växjö|Växjö Cathedral School]], graduating in 1910.

He continued his studies at [[Uppsala University]], being one of the active members of the Uppsala Mathematical Society. Kjellberg recalls: 
<blockquote>He was a genius! My older friends in Uppsala used to tell me about the wonderful years they had had when Carleman was there. He was the most active speaker in the Uppsala Mathematical Society and a well-trained gymnast. When people left the seminar crossing the [[Fyris River]], he walked on his hands on the railing of the bridge.<ref>{{cite book|first=B.|last=Kjellberg|chapter=Mathematicians in Uppsala &mdash; some recollections|language=Swedish|editor=A. Vretblad|title=Festschrift in honour of Lennart Carleson and Yngve Domar|series=Proc. Conf. at Dept. of Math.|publisher=Uppsala Univ.|location=Uppsala|year=1995|pages=87&ndash;95}}</ref></blockquote>

From 1917 he was docent at Uppsala University, and from 1923 &mdash; a full professor at [[Lund University]]. In 1924 he was appointed professor at [[Stockholm University]]. He was elected a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in 1926 and of the [[Finnish Society of Sciences and Letters]] in 1934.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Societas Scientiarum Fennica Årsbok – Vuosikirja 1934-1935 |publisher=Societas Scientiarum Fennica |year=1935 |location=Helsingfors |pages=17}}</ref> From 1927, he was director of the [[Mittag-Leffler Institute]] and editor of [[Acta Mathematica]].<ref name = carlson/>

From  1929 to 1946 Carleman was married to Anna-Lisa Lemming (1885&ndash;1954),<ref>Swedish Death Index, which is a Windows based digital data base, shows different dates (1940 and 1946) of their divorce; {{harvtxt|Maligranda|2003}} lists the year of divorce as 1940. Her original name was Anna Lovisa Lemming, born July 20, 1885.</ref>  the half-sister<ref>Thus according to the [http://search.ancestry.com/search/db.aspx?dbid=2262 Swedish Church birth records]. Note that several sources, including  {{harvtxt|Maligranda|2003}}, state that she was the daughter of Eric Lemming.</ref> of the athlete [[Eric Lemming]]  who won four golden medals and three bronze at the Olympic Games.<ref>[http://www.sok.se/5.e6c6d71083860e1fa80003820.html Webpage of the Swedish Olympic Committee] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120523213321/http://www.sok.se/5.e6c6d71083860e1fa80003820.html |date=2012-05-23 }}</ref> During this period he was also known as a recognized fascist, anti-semite and xenophobe. His interaction with [[William Feller]] before the former departure to the United States was not particularly pleasant, at some point being reported due to his opinion that "Jews and foreigners should be [[execution|executed]]".<ref>{{cite book|mr=2522825|last=Siegmund-Schultze|first=Reinhard|title=Mathematicians fleeing from Nazi Germany: Individual fates and global impact|publisher=Princeton University Press|location=Princeton, New Jersey|year=2009|pages=135|isbn=978-0-691-14041-4}}</ref>

Carlson remembers Carleman as: "secluded and taciturn, who looked at life and people with a bitter humour. In his heart, he was inclined to kindliness towards those around him, and strove to assist them swiftly."<ref name=carlson/> Towards the end of his life, he remarked to his students that "professors ought to be shot at the age of fifty."<ref>{{cite book|mr=1488153|last=Gårding|first=Lars|author-link=Lars Gårding|title=Mathematics and mathematicians. Mathematics in Sweden before 1950.|series=History of Mathematics|year=1998|volume=13|publisher=American Mathematical Society|location=Providence, RI|isbn=0-8218-0612-2|page=[https://archive.org/details/mathematicsmathe0013gard/page/206 206]|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicsmathe0013gard/page/206}}</ref>

During the last decades of his life, Carleman abused alcohol, according to [[Norbert&nbsp;Wiener]]<ref>
"He died of drink<!-- — not the social drinking which leads so often to ruin here—but the fiery, passionate dipsomania which is a common disease even in the very best circles of the Scandinavian countries -->.... During meetings he was often a&nbsp;bit&nbsp;drunk, and afterwards in&nbsp;Paris I saw him come to Mandelbrojt's apartment for an advance on the travel&nbsp;money due&nbsp;him, red-eyed, with a three-day beard." {{cite book|first=Norbert|last=Wiener|author-link=Norbert Wiener|edition=later republished by MIT Press|mr=77455|title=I am a mathematician: The later life of a prodigy|publisher= Doubleday and&nbsp;Co.|location=Garden City,&nbsp;N.&nbsp;Y.|pages=317–318|year=1956|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a4jgAAAAMAAJ&q=Carleman%2C+drink}} {{isbn|9780026273008}}.
<br />
 The mathematician [[Szolem Mandelbrojt]] was an uncle of [[Benoit Mandelbrot]].
</ref><ref name="Maligranda"/> and [[William&nbsp;Feller]].<ref><!-- According to --> {{cite book|last=Siegmund-Schultze|first=R.|year=2009|title= Mathematicians fleeing from Nazi Germany: Individual fates and global impact|location=Princeton, New Jersey|publisher= Princeton University Press|page=135|mr=252285|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rdDvIYYTtrgC&q=Feller%2C+Carleman|chapter=Alternative (non-American) host countries|isbn=978-1400831401}}<!-- , [[William Feller]] wrote to [[Richard Courant]]: "I never catch a glimpse of pure mathematics, partly because it virtually does not
exist as a university institution—the students are learning on their own, the professors are only doing the exams—partly because Carleman is of the touching [rührend] opinion that one should execute [an die Wand stellen] all Jews and immigrants (which, however, he only tells his assistant after consuming a nonnegative [nichtnegativ] amount of alcohol)". --></ref> His final years were plagued by [[neuralgia]]. At the end of 1948, he developed the liver disease [[jaundice]]; he died from complications of the disease.<ref name=carlson/><ref name="Maligranda" >
{{citation|chapter-url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Carleman.html|chapter=Torsten Carleman|first=Lech|last=Maligranda|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews, Scotland|title=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive|The MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]|year=2003|access-date=13 December 2011}}
</ref>
